text: This is the moment every by coder lives for. You told AI what to build and it built it. And then it all broke. Why? Three days ago, we discovered AI coding and it felt like magic. Type what you want. AI builds it, a to do app, done. A database, done. A login page with auth, done. By day three, she had a thousand lines of code across a dozen files. She couldn't explain what any of it did, but it ran, so she assumed it worked. She never asked herself one question. The only question that matters. What am I building? Let's talk about buildings, real ones. When you build a house, you start with a blueprint. It tells you the order. Foundation. Then the frame. Then bowls. Roof. Done. It stands because every piece knows where it goes. The blueprint told it. Now, take away the blueprint. No plan, no order. Start stacking. A wall before there's a foundation. A roof before there are walls. Three different staircases going to the same floor. It looks like a building. Kinda, if you squint. And then SAT. Everything falls down. That's what happened to V's code. She stacked blocks without a blueprint and the tower fell. So what's the blueprint for? A spec. And before you close this table, a spec is not a 100 page document. It's not a JIRA board. It's not a meeting that should have been an email. A spec is one sentence. What am I building and why? That's it. One sentence. Everything else follows from that. Think of it like this. You don't start with a car, you start with a skateboard. Then a bicycle. Then a car. Each version works. Each version moves, but each one is a complete thing re-rode, not a random pile of car parts. Without a spec, you get this. Parts, not a vehicle. Parts that don't connect, built by an AI that doesn't know what the finished thing looks like because you never told it. The spec gives you three things. One, a filter. When AI suggests something, you can ask for a second, does this help me build my skateboard? If no, skip it. To a sequence, foundation, then frame, then walls, then roof. You know the order. Through a definition of done, you know when to stop because you know what finished looks like. Without those three things, you're stacking random blocks and hoping they hold. Back to the present. She stopped coding and she started thinking. One sentence, that's all it took. Same errors, same wall of red, but now one line jumps out because now she knows what she's looking for. Everything is still broken. But now she knows what to fix. At least she thinks she does. Next time, Piers say how she writes 15 pages of specs and somehow that makes everything worse.
